title: HE HAD THE POWER TO FREE PAUL, BUT HE COULDN’T FREE HIMSELF FROM SIN.
paragraphs: HE HAD THE POWER TO FREE PAUL, BUT HE COULDN’T FREE HIMSELF FROM SIN.
A Roman governor brought his wife to hear about Jesus Christ. But when the Gospel confronted his conscience, he made a decision that millions of people are still making today.
Imagine sitting close enough to hear the truth that could change your eternity—and asking it to come back another day.
Not because you didn't understand it.
Not because it wasn't convincing.
But because surrendering to it would mean confronting the very life you had become comfortable living.
That is what makes the encounter between Paul, Felix, and Drusilla one of the most unsettling moments recorded in the book of Acts.
It is not merely a story about an ancient Roman governor.
It is a mirror held before every human soul that wants the comfort of Christianity without the consequences of surrendering to Christ.
Acts 24:24–25 records:

“And after certain days, when Felix came with his wife Drusilla, which was a Jewess, he sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ. And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee.” — Acts 24:24–25, KJV
Read that again.
The prisoner was preaching.
The governor was trembling.
The man who possessed political authority was being confronted by a truth over which he possessed no authority whatsoever.
Felix could command soldiers. He could influence legal proceedings. He could keep Paul imprisoned. He occupied a position that many people would have sacrificed almost anything to obtain.
Yet none of that could silence the reality of his accountability before God.
And beside him sat Drusilla.

She was no ordinary woman. She was the daughter of Herod Agrippa I, the ruler whose persecution of the early Church is recorded in Acts 12. According to the first-century Jewish historian Flavius Josephus, Drusilla had previously been married to Azizus, king of Emesa, before leaving that marriage to become the wife of Felix (Antiquities of the Jews, 20.7.1–2).
Their marriage carried a complicated history.
Their position carried privilege.
Their encounter with Paul carried eternal significance.
Scripture does not record every word Paul spoke that day. Neither does it reveal Drusilla's personal reaction. But Luke deliberately preserves three subjects that Paul addressed.
Righteousness.
Self-control.
The coming judgment.
In the original Greek, Acts 24:25 reads:
Περὶ δικαιοσύνης καὶ ἐγκρατείας καὶ τοῦ κρίματος τοῦ μέλλοντος.
Concerning righteousness, self-control, and the judgment that is to come.
The word δικαιοσύνη (dikaiosynē) refers to righteousness or justice. In this context, it confronts the question of what is right before God, not merely what society considers acceptable.
The word ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia) means self-control—the restraint and mastery of one's desires and impulses. It is also identified as part of the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23.
And κρίμα (krima), in the phrase describing the coming judgment, points toward the reality of divine judgment.
Paul was speaking about matters that no amount of wealth, influence, political authority, or social recognition could make irrelevant.
He was not there to entertain powerful people.
He was not adjusting the Gospel to protect his own interests.
He was not offering Felix a version of Christianity that would leave his conscience undisturbed.
Paul was a prisoner who understood that faithfulness to Jesus Christ mattered more than securing the approval of the man who could release him.
What a contrast to a generation that sometimes wants preachers to make sin sound harmless, repentance sound optional, holiness sound outdated, and judgment disappear from the conversation altogether.
We want a Jesus who blesses our plans but never interrupts them.
A Jesus who heals our wounds but never exposes the wounds we inflict upon others.
A Jesus who forgives our sins but never asks us to turn away from them.
A Jesus who promises heaven without challenging the idols we have built on earth.
But that is not the fullness of the biblical Gospel.
Jesus Himself declared:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15
The Greek word translated as repent is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), a command calling people to repentance—a change of mind and orientation that involves turning toward God.
Repentance is more than feeling embarrassed about being exposed. It is more than crying during worship. It is more than regretting the consequences of our decisions.
It is a turning that reaches into the direction of our lives.
And genuine repentance is not an attempt to purchase God's forgiveness through human effort. It is our response to His mercy, inseparably connected to faith in Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters because Felix experienced something that many people mistakenly confuse with transformation.
He became afraid.
Luke uses the Greek expression ἔμφοβος γενόμενος (emphobos genomenos), meaning that Felix became frightened or alarmed.
The Gospel had disturbed him.
But being disturbed by the truth is not the same as surrendering to it.
You can tremble under conviction and still protect your rebellion.
You can cry during a sermon and return to the same secret compromise.
You can acknowledge that Scripture is right while continually refusing to live under its authority.
You can be emotionally moved without being spiritually transformed.
Perhaps that is why this story feels so painfully familiar.
Maybe you have been telling yourself that you will finally surrender to Jesus when your life becomes less complicated.
When the relationship ends.
When the business becomes stable.
When the money arrives.
When the addiction becomes easier to overcome.
When your children grow older.
When you have finished enjoying the things you already know are pulling you away from God.
You keep promising Him a future version of yourself while withholding the person you are today.
And without realizing it, you are repeating the response of Felix.
“When I have a convenient season, I will call for thee.”
The original Greek contains the expression καιρὸν δὲ μεταλαβών (kairon de metalabōn), conveying the idea of obtaining a suitable opportunity.
Felix postponed the conversation.
He wanted another occasion.
Another time.
A more convenient moment.
But when has surrendering our deepest idols ever been convenient?
When has confronting pride, dishonesty, bitterness, sexual immorality, greed, unforgiveness, or hidden rebellion ever felt comfortable?
If you are waiting for obedience to become convenient before you obey, you may spend your entire life waiting.
One of the most dangerous words in a person's spiritual life is not necessarily “never.” Sometimes, it is “later.”
Later sounds reasonable.
Later allows us to acknowledge the truth without immediately responding to it.
Later lets us preserve the appearance of faith while protecting the habits that contradict it.
Later can become the respectable language of spiritual resistance.
And the frightening thing about postponement is that every repeated refusal can make the next refusal easier.
Hebrews 3:15 warns:
“To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.”
Not when everything is perfect.
Not when obedience costs you nothing.
Today.
You do not need to publicly disclose your private struggles. Let those words express a sincere desire to stop running from what God has been showing you.
But the story of Felix becomes even more disturbing when we continue reading.
Acts 24:26 reveals that Felix also hoped Paul would give him money. He frequently summoned Paul and conversed with him.
Think about that.
Felix continued having access to a man who preached Jesus Christ.
He continued having opportunities to hear.
Yet Luke reveals that financial self-interest was also influencing his behavior.
Two years later, according to Acts 24:27, Felix left Paul imprisoned because he wanted to gain favor with the Jews.
The biblical record gives us no account of Felix repenting or placing his faith in Jesus Christ.
We cannot claim to know his ultimate eternal destiny. That belongs to God's judgment. But we can recognize the warning preserved in Scripture.
Repeated exposure to the Gospel does not automatically produce repentance.
You can attend church for decades.
You can memorize Scripture.
You can surround yourself with Christian friends, share Bible verses, listen to worship music, and know exactly how to speak the language of faith.
Yet familiarity with Christianity must never be mistaken for reconciliation with God through Christ.
There is a difference between knowing about Jesus and trusting Jesus.
Between admiring His teachings and submitting to His lordship.
Between wanting relief from guilt and receiving the grace that calls us into a transformed life.
And here is where the story becomes more than a warning.
Because the man preaching to Felix had once carried a scandalous history of his own.
Paul had not always been an apostle.
He had persecuted the Church.
He had approved of Stephen's killing.
He had entered homes and dragged believers away to prison.
Acts 8:1–3 and Acts 9:1–6 preserve the uncomfortable truth about the man who would later become one of Christianity's most influential missionaries.
Paul understood what it meant to be wrong while believing he was right.
He understood religious zeal without a proper understanding of Jesus.
He understood the devastating reality of having a past that could not be undone.
Yet Jesus met him.
Jesus confronted him.
Jesus redirected his life.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The man who once sought to imprison Christians eventually endured imprisonment for proclaiming Christ.
The hands once associated with persecution became instruments of Gospel ministry.
Paul did not stand before Felix as a man who had never needed mercy.
He stood there as living evidence of what mercy could accomplish.
In 1 Timothy 1:15, Paul writes:
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not the celebration of morally superior people.
Not the condemnation of broken people without hope.
Not the illusion that we can clean ourselves sufficiently to deserve God's acceptance.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He bore our sins upon the cross. He died and rose again, providing the foundation of our forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life through faith in Him.
The righteousness we desperately need is not something we can manufacture through religious performance.
Romans 3:23–24 teaches that all have sinned and that believers are justified freely by God's grace through the redemption found in Christ Jesus.
This is why the message of coming judgment is not separated from the message of grace.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing depth of God's love.
Sin is not insignificant.
Grace is not permission to continue in rebellion.
And repentance is not the enemy of mercy.
Romans 2:4 tells us that the goodness of God leads us to repentance.
The Savior who confronts your sin is also the Savior who offers forgiveness.
The One who calls you out of darkness is the One who makes a new life possible.
Perhaps you are reading this with a history you are ashamed of.
Perhaps there are messages you have deleted, promises you have broken, relationships you have damaged, people you have betrayed, or decisions you desperately wish you could reverse.
Perhaps the person everyone admires publicly is struggling with something nobody knows privately.
You may have become exceptionally skilled at appearing spiritually healthy while quietly avoiding the very places where you need God's healing.
But you cannot heal what you continually refuse to bring before Him.
And you do not need to pretend that your past was innocent for Jesus to redeem your life.
Paul's testimony proves that a scandalous past does not place someone beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
That does not mean grace erases every earthly consequence. Repentance may require confession, accountability, restitution, changed behavior, and accepting responsibility for the harm we have caused.
But your worst chapter does not have to determine the direction of every chapter that follows.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending the sin never happened.
He transforms sinners through forgiveness, redemption, and new life.
He does not call evil good.
He calls people out of evil and into His marvelous light.
He does not merely offer a better public image.
He offers reconciliation with God and a transformed heart.
Felix had the opportunity to hear about that Savior.
So did Drusilla.
And now, through the testimony preserved in Scripture, so do you.
The question is no longer simply what Felix did with the Gospel.
The question is what you are doing with it.
What have you been postponing?
What has God been confronting through His Word that you keep explaining away?
What compromise have you renamed because calling it sin would require you to confront it?
What part of your life have you been asking Jesus to bless while refusing to surrender it to Him?
You may not have tomorrow to make the decision you are avoiding today.
Scripture reminds us:
“Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” — 2 Corinthians 6:2
Come to Christ.
Not because you have finally become worthy.
Not because you have successfully repaired every broken part of your life.
But because He is the Savior, and His mercy is greater than your ability to save yourself.
If you have been running, return.
If you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you have fallen, confess your sin and seek His forgiveness.
If you have never truly trusted Him, turn to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
There may come a day when temptation, compromise, or spiritual exhaustion makes postponement sound reasonable again.
Return to these words when that happens.
Let us fill more of our digital spaces with Scripture, biblical truth, encouragement, conviction, repentance, and the transforming message of Jesus Christ.
There is already enough content teaching people how to become more successful, more admired, and more comfortable.
We also need content reminding people how deeply they need their Savior.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that believers should give willingly rather than under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But the greater purpose is not merchandise.
It is ministry.
It is helping more people encounter biblical truth in a world where distraction, compromise, and spiritual confusion compete for their attention every day.
Give freely, prayerfully, and with a willing heart.
Because when this life is over, the greatest achievement will not be how many people knew our names.
It will not be how much influence we accumulated, how many possessions we acquired, or how comfortably we lived.
What matters eternally is our relationship with Jesus Christ.
Felix could dismiss Paul from his presence.
But he could not dismiss his accountability before God.
He could postpone another conversation.
But he could not command eternity to wait.
Do not make the same mistake.
The Gospel is not merely something to appreciate when life becomes convenient.
It is the good news of the Savior you need today.
Never become so comfortable asking Jesus to wait that you spend your entire life preparing for a surrender you never make.
